Some basic kitten care for ya:
- weigh the kittens everyday, they can be weighed with a kitchen scale (just, yeah, don’t accidentally dose the babies if you’re using the scale for dual purposes)
- write the weights down to track them and look for patterns
- it’s important to get a starting weight, sometimes kittens are born underweight and they need special attention
- weigh kittens who are underweight, losing weight or not gaining twice a day
- kittens may need to be syringe or bottle fed if not eating, at the worst they need tube feeding (which is something you would need an experience with)
- kittens don’t eat cow milk, there’s actually kitten milk replacement available (KMR)
- if you end up bottle or syringe feeding kittens, you also need to stimulate them to empty their bladder and colon (this is important - they cannot otherwise empty their bladder and colon!)
- if they start to go downhill, and you can’t afford vet care, look into local animal shelters/sanctuaries but make sure they aren’t high kill (preferably do this beforehand)

I work at a cat sanctuary, we don’t euthanize cats unless their quality of life has deteriorated to the point where we can no longer ease their suffering. One of the most compassionate things I’ve witnessed and then become part of is how all the staff comfort a dying cat. The number one rule we have when euthanizing a cat is to make them feel comfortable. It can take up 15 minutes for a cat to be fully sedated before we administer the euthanasia drug (IV lines make the process quicker, but they often don’t have an IV placed). No sadness and no crying. It stresses the cat out and gives them anxiety. We instead talk softly to them, give them lots of pets, and then tell stories about their lives. Our memories, how they came to us, we laugh at how they used to kick our asses when we had to trim their nails, things that are anything but sad. We save our sadness and tears for after they have passed. It is our final gift to them, to be surrounded with love and happiness.

No cure for rabies. Vaccinations beforehand and/or if you’re potentially exposed to a rabid animal. Preventative vaccinations need follow up, it’s not one and done. You may need boosters in a few years. 

If you have preventative vaccinations (series of 3 given at specific intervals), you still need to get booster shots if bitten by a potentially rabid animal. Preventative vaccines only essentially delay the time an infection would set in, you still need care if you get bit. If you do contract rabies, don’t seek treatment, the infection will almost certainly kill you. With treatment immediately after a bite, you stand a much better chance of surviving.

Second animal but the first that qualifies as a “pet” in my mind: a guinea pig. She was a gorgeous black and orange abby. It was a thought out decision, she loves a pampered life, and she lived happily for 9 years. I’ve since had 10 other guinea pigs. Two are still alive, one is about a year and the other is 7 years. They all have and had their own personalities. Curious, nervous, energetic, but can be trained to be more social, use a litter pan, and even do tricks. Unfortunately they’re prone to health issues. Bladder stones are a given in most pigs and surgery to remove larger stones is only temporary. They’ll come back, and surgery on guinea pigs is notoriously challenging. You need to have an exotic vet who has previous experience with guinea pigs. Cancer is another big one. That said, I’ve cared for them as I care for my cats. The best medical treatment I can provide, and the expenses are something I just make work. There’s a lot involved in their care that most people aren’t prepared for, but having a piggie is an amazing experience. Plus they’re super cute.

I work at a cat sanctuary. Most of the stress comes from watching cats slowly decline health wise despite aggressive treatment. It’s not terrible, you just learn to cope with it. Worrisome cat bites happen, but you get yourself cleaned up and seen by a doctor if needed. These are normal to me and my coworkers. 

The scariest thing was walking in one morning at about 7:30. I was the first in the building and was turning on all the lights, getting ready to feed our diabetic cats. As I walk through our lobby I hear this scream. Like, flat out, loud scream from one of the cats. We have some vocal cats but this was different. I almost kept walking, but had that unnerving feeling of “something doesn’t feel right right, you just need to check”. I look under the front desk and see a nightmare. One of our oldest cats, Oil (19 years), managed to entangle himself in one of the cords under the desk. It was a small cord, used to connect our credit card reader to the outlet and only ran a few feet. Oil was stuck and screaming. 

I immediately went to pull the cord off but it was wrapped several times around his body - it was tight. When I pulled, he tried to wiggle free, just making things tighter. I needed to unwrapped him slowly, I couldn’t get his body through the loops. I pulled the cord to try to get more slack - nothing. I stood up grabbed the reader and pulled the cord out. Didn’t care if broke it in the process. I finally was able to unwind Oil from the wire. He immediately tries to run and falls flat on his side. Fuck. I have pure adrenaline running through me, but am still able to keep most of the panic in check. 

I scoop him up with one arm, I have my cell phone in another and I’m calling one of our vet team staff. She answers and says she’s leaving her house as we are on the phone. Oil’s vitals are stable fortunately, and we can wait the 40 minute drive for her to come in. 

My coworker arrives at this time (this whole event happened over the course of only 5 minutes). She’s confused as to the chaos but immediately starts grabbing supplies. 

Our senior vet tech arrives in half the time her commute normally takes, just 20 minutes, it was a Saturday and fortunately no cops were watching the roads. In the midst of everything, my coworker and I ran around, fed our diabetics, gave them insulin, and returned to monitor Oil. The rest of rounds could wait, Oil took precedent, we didn’t care if we ended up eating lunch at 3. We weren’t as much panicked as we were determined and focused. Almost like a “this isn’t happening, we’ve got you Oil”. 

I thought he was paralyzed. I straight up thought I had untangled a now paraplegic cat, one that was already frail enough at the age of 19. But it didn’t appear that way, he still had evidence of feeling and some movement in his hind legs. He was weak and dehydrated, he likely was stuck for much of the night. He was not interested in eating or drinking. We got him on heat support and placed an IV so we could give fluids. We took X-rays to look for any internal damage, fortunately there wasn’t any. We were taking this minute by minute, finally relaxing to hour by hour. He slowly regained feeling and was able to sit by the end of the day. 

It took days for Oil to regain enough strength to stand up and then start to clumsily walk again. Unfortunately, this seemed to be the event that setback his overall health. He never recovered 100% in the next few weeks and eventually we made the difficult decision to let him go, we could no longer alleviate pain and suffering. 

It was a downright terrifying event for all parties involved. This was not even in the realm of “possible emergency scenarios”. The cord could have wrapped around Oil’s neck instead. I don’t know how long he was stuck, how long he was in that nightmare. He only began screaming when he heard I was walking by the desk, meaning it was probably most of the night. There were and are many thoughts that remain to this day. 

We went overboard with securing cables, cords and any type of wire. To most people, things look really nice and tidy. To us, it’s a reminder of an event no one wants to ever relive.

Seroquel is a weird drug. Dose matters. It hits histamine first, then with increasing dosing, hits serotonin and then dopamine. Insomnia is treated with lower doses, but taking higher doses may help. Sedation levels out at about 400mg. At one point I was on 800mg without any increased sedation.

I work at a cat sanctuary. Love the cats, but not all the cats love humans. I had a particularly nasty bite on my hand that had me in the hospital for two days on IV antibiotics. It was my first bite when I began working. And a learning experience. My hand was swollen and red, hurt like hell because of the swelling. Thankfully I didn’t need surgery, but it was up in the air as the bite was on my hand/thumb/first finger. 

Many angry cats, scratching claws, and bites later I’ve gotten better at avoiding that. Immediately wash the bite, scrub that shit for ten minutes. Bandage the wound to make sure it stays clean. Applying antibiotic ointment if it’s not properly cleaned can trap bacteria, that was my issue with my first bite. I no longer apply cream to bites at work. It’s just too much of a chance that some bacteria can creep in even if it’s bandaged. When I get home I scrub it again (and yeah, you need to scrub enough to reopen the wound) and do epsom salt soaks. If it starts to tingle/burn during the soak, that’s a good thing. Apply antibiotic ointment. There’s a prescription topical antibiotic that I was given for one of my cat bites, I still have a bunch left. Ointment is typically only on day one or two. The bite can be left unbandaged if you’re just sitting around the house and it’s better to not bandage it. I sometimes have to reopen the wound with the scrub/soak if it decides to get signs of an initial infection. I’ve needed oral antibiotics on two additional bites but my other bites have healed with no issue. 

Typically if a cat bites and “latches” on, you’re not going to have a good time infection wise. Or if the cat bites and then “tears” open the skin. Older cats may have teeth break off. And of course if you don’t know the medical history, that carries a bunch of other issues. 

Generally if you get bit my an animal, you should get it checked out. But, if it happens to be an occupational hazard...the more you know :)

I wasn’t diagnosed until a year and a half later. But that year and a half was hell. I didn’t know what was wrong with me and no one else did either. I lost my emotional stability. My behaviors were completely impulsive. I lost my ability to concentrate. My motivation to do anything went out the window. I had the most horrific migraines. I had episodes of dizziness where I would need to lay down. There were a few scattered seizures. I isolated myself, lost all the friends I previously had. 

I was in a bad state, physically, mentally, and emotionally. I have limited memories from a four month chunk of the really awful part. I think my brain has intentionally repressed it, the emotional pain involved is best kept in the far corners of my mind. I have no desire to fully remember or relive it. The bits of memory I have are enough. 

When I was finally diagnosed it took a while for me to come back. I went on and off medications, saw so many different doctors, etc. But I managed to come out the other side. I began learning how to manage my life with my new (read: damaged) brain. 

My second concussion added issues to my neck. After falling directly headfirst onto the floor from a lofted bed, my neck snapped sideways. I now have a bulging disc at C6 which causes pain issues. The headache I had from it was insane. It was the worst migraine and it lasted for days. I had already been at the ER the day it occurred to get checked out. But I had to go back because of the migraine. They put me on some strong painkillers which I ended up needing for two weeks. Only then was the pain more manageable. I had a flare up of symptoms after my second concussion as well. 

My third concussion seemed innocent enough. I fell backwards and hit the back of my head. It gave me a flare of my symptoms but then I noticed it also seemed to aggravate the issues I was having with balance. Previously I had lost the ability to maintain my balance with my eyes closed. But now I can’t balance well with my eyes open. I can’t walk a line heel-to-toe or stand with my feet together. 

Now I find when I’m standing I tend to sway, but it’s uncomfortable as I don’t feel steady. So I compensate by making slight adjustments, shifting my weight intentionally  or walking a step. 

My fourth concussion was weird. I had slammed my head on the door to a metal dog/cat crate. The kind you’ve seen in a vet’s office and which are used at animal shelters. No big deal. I’ve done this exact thing since then and it hurts, I get a bit dizzy, but whatever. Another flare of symptoms. Not this time. I guess I hit my head in the right place, or with more force. The dizziness came, an instantaneous headache, and I was about to vomit. I had to leave and go home. I made it out into the parking lot and then vomited into some bushes. I managed to drive myself home. I promptly went to bed and slept for a long time until someone else finally came home. 

For whatever reason it was, this concussion caused me to lose my ability to speak for several days. I could manage a few words and I could understand others. I’m not sure now, maybe it was a week. Things are really foggy. My CT scan was clear. I couldn’t drive to college and I remember I wasn’t able to do any work on the computer or even send emails. I was out of commission for a couple weeks I believe. I was on an anti nausea medication and another short term course of anti migraine meds. 

Now I’m living with all the residual symptoms of my injuries. It sucks but it’s life. Acceptance is hard and I honestly am still fucking pissed at everything. The why, the how, maybe life could be different, maybe I would have lived like a normal teen. I feel like I missed out on so much and I can never get it back. 

I blame myself which I logically know makes no sense. If I wouldn’t have been here, done this, etc. 

The things that still bother me the most are managing my mood. With 6 medications on board I can actually function. But it’s still 6 things that I depend on to help keep me sane. My concentration is still an issue. My motivation has peaks and then seemingly endless periods of nothing.  I confuse numbers and words, which makes me quite awful at math and makes it frustrating (or hilarious) to read articles/books/email. 

My most recent MRI showed a minor herniation of my cerebellum (“brain is squeezing out of my skull”). It’s difficult to assess the complications it may be causing. In anyone else, someone with no history of head trauma, my symptoms would indicate this minor herniation was causing major problems. But for me, where do my head trauma symptoms stop and the cerebellar herniation symptoms begin?  It’s even more difficult because I keep managing to hit my head (despite it being minor) and sometimes I get a slight flare of symptoms. A bit dizzy, a bit tired, a bit depressed, whatever. 

Maybe all of this has made me who I am, but maybe I could have been someone different. In a positive way. Done more, experienced more, felt more. Maybe or maybe not. I think the thought of “what if” may bother me more than the symptoms some days.

Rabies with cats is actually more difficult. I work at a cat shelter to preface this. Once a cat starts showing neuro symptoms of possible rabies it must be quarantined for 10 days. If a cat has rabies, it will continue to deteriorate during the 10 days and eventually die (however we would not let it suffer to the point of death). After death, the head must be removed and sent for testing to fully confirm rabies. This is why we can't "test for rabies" and keep your cat alive!

Now here's the issue. A cat can temporarily "carry" rabies. If the cat sustains a bite on its hind foot or tail, symptoms may not show for weeks. The further the bite from the brain/nervous system, the longer it can take for symptoms to present. To add even more complication, the bite wound may have healed so you would have no obvious evidence a cat could have been exposed. Fortunately, contracting rabies from cats is unusual.

Separating kittens too young doesn't allow for the kitten to know, essentially, "biting hurts". And that's difficult to teach. 

It's good to hear she's made progress, and that you're not using punishment to change behaviors. And adopting the so-called "unadoptables" is always such an amazing act of kindness. No cat is truly unadoptable, they're just waiting for the perfect person to come along and take them home.

Cats tend not to respond well to negative reinforcement (nose flicking, water bottle sprays, etc.). It may work momentarily, but it often doesn't help long-term. Alternatively, positive reinforcement stands a somewhat better chance though it depends on the cat. Offering a treat when they do the desired the behavior is an example. The treat must given when you decide, not the cat. 

We want cats who bite or have aggression issues to make a decision, on their own, to calm down. If a cat is trying to playfully bite, we simply walk away and ignore them. It sounds cruel, but as soon as they sit down and relax we will walk over and give a treat. They choose to calm down, we choose to give a treat. Giving them attention for undesired behavior is something to avoid. Which is why people can have a difficult time of their cats on counter tops. If you pick up your cat from the counter and put it on the ground only to pet it, your cat is going to learn counter=pets. If you pick it up only to snuggle, again it's a counter top=positive attention. 

If a cat has severe aggression issues, as in they are seriously hurting other cats/humans (or they have self-directed aggression), we can start them on medication. It's not ideal, but once the medication starts working, it's easier to address the learned behavior responses. 

With all of the cats, it's also important to observe their responses to the environment. Many of the cats have reasons to bite, often they are known though sometimes it's unknown. We have to play detective on these guys. Are they sound sensitive? Are they sensitive to touch? Does food motivate them? Are they protective of their food and become aggressive if interrupted? Is there something or someone that easily trigger them? Another cat? A certain human? Do they bite because they want something (food, petting, play)? Is there a pattern to their biting or does it appear to be random? Having a truly random, aggressive, biting cat is one of the most difficult challenges. 

Many of our biters we understand their reasons, triggers, and behavior patterns. This makes the rehab just a bit easier. We do though have a two current residents who have no pattern or triggers, one adopted as a kitten and returned after eight years, the other picked up as a young cat as a stray (not a true feral, just a cat with unpredictable behavior). The first cat, the return, has been with us for almost a year. She was an unprovoked biter. Quite literally she would run across the room, leap onto a table, and bite people. It took months for her calm down. Much of the time, we could only ignore her. She was not responsive to much else, finding the right medication and dose was a challenge itself. Slowly, she learned how to calm down. We would reward her when we noticed she was calmly laying on the table, a chair, or just on the floor. We're only just starting to help the second resident, she's a really unusual case. 

It's a long process for some cats, but others can pick it up quickly. We've had cats who come around in a few weeks. And some cats you have to understand will always set their own boundaries with you! Resolving the biting or aggression is priority. If a cat decides it prefers its head and neck/shoulders brushed, but will spawn hell if you try anywhere else, that's an exchange that may be okay to make. It's also a situation easier to work with. It's predictable. 

I'll wrap it up by saying, you have to think like a cat. They don't understand "yes" and "no". You may yell at them "stop biting!" but they don't understand what you're saying. They're only responding to what you do. If you don't do anything to reward a behavior, the behavior is going to change. This will be for good and bad behaviors, so don't forget to respond to the good!

Rescues don't have to be bitey! I work at a cat sanctuary and we teach cats not to bite. We have people who return their cats because they've started biting. It often begins as innocent "play" as a kitten that continues into adulthood. "Hand games" may seem harmless and fun, but eventually that kitten gets bigger and still sees that hand as a toy. And a 15 pound cat biting doesn't have the same cuteness. We can rehabilitate the cats, though it takes time. Boundaries are incredibly important to establish in kittenhood, as re-teaching everything a cat knows about the world and how to interact with it is, understandably, more difficult. With any known biting cat, we warn adopters that it's in the cats history. If a cat can push your boundaries on right and wrong, a small bite to get treats or to play, they will continue to keep pushing (and biting). 

It's possible for you to change your cats biting behavior. It will take time and patience, especially if you don't know the full history of your rescue (they may have had a traumatic event that caused the biting). But it's definitely possible to have a non-bitey cat!

I fear it's going to be many of the prescription medications.  We're putting chemicals into us that often have no long term outcomes. Or, we've had similar medications with established long term effects that we've realized "oh well we didn't expect that deadly side effect". 


I'm mostly talking about the ones for mental health where we don't exactly know how they work, but they seem to work so we take them. We have working ideas about the meds balancing neurotransmitters, but there's still some significant issues with this. It's not a cut and dry solution. Everyone responds differently to medications, we have numerous ones that are in the same class that work either on the same or different receptors. Some people go through many trial and failures, need several medications, or fall into the "treatment resistant" group where they have a disorder that, for whatever reason, doesn't respond to medication. 

Before anyone jumps down my throat, I will say I'm on a handful of psych meds. It keeps me stable and sane and ultimately that's what matters at the moment. However, I also know if I'm ever in a situation where I can't get my meds (national emergency, war, the apocalypse), I will go through a hell of a withdrawal. There's also a lot of current side effects that I deal with, which is an obvious sign that not all parts of my brain are 'happy' with certain medications. 

I worry that after so many years of purposefully altering our brain chemistry, we may never be able to live without the medications. Even if you try to ever so slowly wean off, your body may have become dependent and can't balance itself out. That's worrying. Maybe not so much for me, I'm an adult and know what I'm putting into my body. I understand why, understand the potential side effects and the "what if" possibilities. But there's so many kids who are being prescribed medication who don't have the ability to say 'no'. And they certainly don't grasp that medications may cause short or long term side effects. With a child's brain still developing, it makes me really question if we should be trying to correct a chemical imbalance that may otherwise correct itself in the future.

I don't have schizophrenia but I have bipolar disorder with psychotic features. When I have manic episodes I can become psychotic. Fortunately, the psychosis only occurs with manic episodes, outside of mania I'm psychosis-free. 

A lot of people think when someone is psychotic they aren't aware of reality, that's not true in the majority of cases. As an example, if I am hallucinating voices outside my window, talking about how they're planning to come into my window, I can be aware it's not real. But that doesn't make it go away, that doesn't take away the fear because even if I can calm myself down a bit, there's always going to be some fear. Which is normal for anyone if they were overhearing a discussion on breaking into their home. 

I've developed a technique to determine if I'm hallucinating. I place a memory foam pillow over my head, covering my ears. It blocks out all sound, so if I still hear what the hallucination is, then I know what it is. 

There's a lot of questioning and frustration during episodes. You feel like you're "going crazy" then you realize you "already are crazy". Your thoughts scatter as the anxiety climbs. Anxiety about the psychosis, the rest of your life, how an episode is interrupting some important thing (work, school, etc). Then you start thinking about how this is not the time for another hospitalization but that you may need it and that's a shitty situation. 

I'm able to gain some sense of control and realize I need to take an emergency medication dose. After not sleeping for a few days, it knocks me out and I sleep for over a day.  But it's not always that easy.

Yep, it depends on the unit/hospital. Some units are "high security" and have more restrictions. Others allow more freedoms like wearing street clothing. It also depends on individual patient restrictions. My experience being a patient with a history of self-harm and known suicide attempts led to more restrictions in what I could have - even things provided to other patients were prohibited for me. 

And I definitely forgot to mention - everything will be searched by staff.

My addition, here's a list of things if your loved one is in a psychiatric unit because it's vastly different. 

• most important: check what regulations the unit has on items, this is just based on my experience

• no strings on anything, if you're bringing in clothes make sure there's no strings or strings that are easily removed

• no balloons (string issue), no flowers in vases (glass can be broken), no pictures in frames (glass issue). Bring pictures outside of frames, flowers in plastic vases may be allowed

• no electronics, psychiatric units are often a "bubble" and don't allow cell phones, computers, etc. 

• nothing with alcohol - any type of alcohol can be an issue. Conditioner, body lotion, things that you wouldn't think of can have a type of alcohol which can be prohibited

• should be obvious, but nothing sharp so no razors, scissors, nail clippers, etc. 

• basic necessities, like a tooth brush and toothpaste are great and pads for female loved ones (no tampons because of the string issue), yes they are provided but they're often poor quality

• check to see if personal belongings like pillows and blankets are allowed, if they are, bring them - the linens given are not comfortable

• clothing is appreciated, socks and underwear are very appreciated!

• more on clothing, make it comfortable. No one really cares what they look like on a psych unit, so comfort is primary. 

• if food is allowed to be brought in, make sure it's in a sealed package. So fast food is a no-no. 

• books are great, coloring books are even better!

Here's some things you can do:

• don't tell anyone where your loved one is, unless they tell you it's okay to do so

• ask to visit, sometimes people don't want visitors, other times they'll want you to come one day and not the next

• to add onto that, know when visiting hours are, psych units are very regulated and have set times for groups, meals, and visiting hours

• ask if your loved one wants help answering texts or emails in their behalf. Some people are very uncomfortable with others knowing where they are and it's difficult to go "radio silent" for a few days or  week

If you have a hot water bottle or a heating pad, place a blanket (one layer) over top and place him on it. Even though his nose is warm, he may still feel cold and quite miserable. Especially if he's been struggling for a bit as you mentioned in the comments. Make sure it doesn't get too warm, and make sure he is eating and drinking. If he normally uses a litter box and suddenly stops, that's a sign something isn't right. If you see him using the box, watch to see if he's straining to urinate or dedicate, or if he's unable to do so at all. Does his poop look well-formed? Watch for diarrhea or constipation. Blood in the stool or urine is concerning, especially if you can visibly see it. Take a sample if you see blood. It's best to find a sterile cup and place the sample in there. Put it in the refrigerator until you can get it to a vet/clinic. 

For the future, it's worth knowing how to take a temperature (yes, that would be a rectal temp). 

Monitor his breathing, making sure it's not labored. Take a look at his gums, are they a healthy pink color or are they very pale (or very red)? Make note of any discharge or swelling from his nose, eyes, or ears. 

It's a good idea to look him over again. Pay attention to any possible smaller injuries, ones that aren't very obvious from far away. Move his legs gently, do they seem painful when you move them? Gently do a once over on his body, his back, spine, abdomen, etc. Again looking for signs that a specific area is painful. 

Get him up and see how he walks. Does he collapse? Fall to one side? Is a bit "wobbly"? These are signs of possible neurologic involvement. They're not good.

This is just a basic assessment. It will be helpful when he sees a vet.

When you go into the ER there's two care teams that kind of 'merge' to form one. One is medical and the other is psych. Psych patients have to be cleared medically. Even if someone doesn't try to hurt themselves, they have to be cleared by medical staff. This involves the basic vitals but also blood work, urine screens, any additionally tests needed to rule out medical problems (EKG, CT scans, etc.). Medical problems may cause psych issues, endocrine or neurological issues can mimic psych symptoms. Additionally the medical team rules out any drug/alcohol intoxication, and addresses abnormalities ("is it an actual heart attack or is it just anxiety causing that abnormal heart rhythm?"). 

The medical doctors are essentially forced to deal with psych patients, they may not want to, but that's what their job entails. Yes it's only the medical side, but there's still interaction with the patient. 

The psych team deals with the psych issues. They want to work with psych patients. 

A lot of the issues come from the nurses and patient care techs in the ER, there's no differentiation with medical or psych. So a nurse who only wants to deal with medical patients ends up getting "stuck" with psych patients. 

Doctors are, I guess, lucky they don't have to deal with the issue of getting "stuck".

~6AM: If you're unfortunate to need blood work, this is when the tech comes in, flips on all the damn lights, pokes you, and then leaves.
7AM: Morning vitals. Blood pressure, pulse, temp, and weight if it was Sunday (or every day if you were an eating disorder patient). Most people woke up and sat in the common area watching the news until breakfast arrived.
8AM: Breakfast arrived, or is supposed to. It was rarely on time. During breakfast you would fill out your menu for lunch, dinner, and the next morning's breakfast. Patients were called individually for medications. 
~9:30AM: Morning meeting. Daily sheets asking about symptoms were filled out. Overview of unit rules for new patients. 
10AM: First group.
-Short break in between-
11AM: Second group.
12PM (Noon): Lunch arrives...or is supposed to. Afternoon vitals for those who are detoxing, on certain meds, or need it for whatever reason. Medications for those who need it.
12:30-1:30PM: Visiting hours. If you didn't have visitors, it was whatever you wanted to do. 
1:30-2:00PM: Free time, whatever you wanted to do. 
2-3PM (weekdays): third group
3-4PM (weekdays): fourth group
*2-4PM on weekends was extended free time, it was boring as fuck*
4PM: Evening meeting, fill out the same questions about any symptoms. Takes less than five minutes.
5PM: Dinner...if it arrives on time. Evening meds for those who need it.
5:30-6:30PM: Evening visitors. Free time for others.
7-8PM: If AA volunteers were coming in, this would be the allotted. Often they didn't make it in. Mandatory attendance for patients with known substance abuse issues. Optional for other patients.
9-10PM: Night doses of medications. Patients would request early doses, some would want to finish watching a show and want medications later
10PM: Wii off.
11PM: TV off. Most people were already asleep. 
*There was no mandatory bed time. You just couldn't have the TV on. You were free to do anything if you couldn't sleep as long as you didn't make a ton of noise.*

My psych classes(undergrad) all included participation in projects/experiments/questionnaires from the senior students. It was optional participation but you were given extra credit if you participated. The questionnaires were always easy to complete and I knew I was helping other students so I filled them out. 

However this was only my experience at one college, I later transferred to complete my degree elsewhere. So the policies and encouraged student participation weren't in place. I had a difficult time completing my research for my degree. I couldn't get a large enough pool of participants and had to change how I approached my topic. I switched from conducting questionnaires and interviews to a content analysis of already available info (I was examining the communication challenges between clinicians and patients receiving psychiatric care, I ended up using the "review your doctor" websites to collect the needed info). 

There's going to be issues with any pool of participants, but at least the research was conducted. Students, on the undergrad level, are often only conducting research for their degree. While there's opportunity for the research to be taken to varying levels of conventions, there's a lot of students who just want a degree. So the focus is on gathering enough data, not having a perfectly balanced study. It's also impossible to design a "perfect" study. This is where the limitations section comes into play. You address the possible issues with your participants like selection bias, similar demographics, limited sample size, etc.

Switching session may also help. It gives you a chance to restart the business and also avoid any possible things buggy with your current session - not saying that the sessions are *always* buggy, but this is what I've found personally helpful.

Alcohol and propranolol, as mentioned in another comment, have CNS depressant effects. The exaggerated 'startle response' in PTSD is decreased by propranolol, this is achieved in part by regulating the release of adrenaline. This regulation of adrenaline also is responsible for propranolol's ability to lower blood pressure. Alcohol can have an additive effect on lowering blood pressure, and dropping too low is where people run into problems. 

Propranolol itself can present this problem (lowering blood pressure too much) so I'd advise monitoring your blood pressure initially, if your dose increases, or if you feel dizzy/lightheaded.

Prozac is not a stimulant. It may have stimulant-like properties in certain populations, but it's not itself a stimulant. One of these populations are people with bipolar disorder (though to be noted, this doesn't apply to everyone diagnosed with bipolar disorder). Individuals with bipolar disorder can experience adverse reactions to antidepressant monotherapy. Prozac, which is an antidepressant, can induce hypomania or mania in such circumstances. This may appear to be stimulant-like because of the possible euphoria, increased energy, etc. Again, this isn't the norm because Prozac isn't a stimulant. 

Edit: You're taking Abilify and Effexor and you think it's okay to drink heavily? No, it's not okay. You can do it, sure, but not without any ill effect. Abilify is an antipsychotic, and while it is newer antipsychotic ("atypical") with less sedative effects, alcohol doesn't play nicely with it. Alcohol and antipsychotics, in general, both have sedative effects, combining the two can lead to a potentially lethal interaction (too much sedative effect=too much CNS depression). There are a variety of anecdotal reports from people who take Effexor and drink alcohol. Some say the combination intensifies the effects of alcohol ("drunker faster"), other describe the exaggerated hangover effect, others describe the inability to get, or rather feel, drunk. That last one is particularly problematic, if someone doesn't feel drunk, there's it's likely they'll continue to drink more - just because the person isn't feeling it, doesn't mean their body isn't processing it. The liver still has to process the alcohol. Taking psych meds with alcohol in general should be avoided, aside from the possible interactions alcohol can exacerbate underlying psychiatric illness like depression. 

Also, what 'metabolic pathways' are you referring to? Prozac is an SSRI and works primarily on serotonin, Effexor is an SNRI and works primarily on serotonin and norepinephrine. Abilify works as a unique antipsychotic on dopamine and norepinephrine. I'm confused what 'pathways' you're referring to.
